claims.claim: Bone homeostasis is regulated by growth factors and cytokines produced within bone and systemic factors such as parathyroid hormone (PTH) and estrogens.
claims.source: This homeostasis is regulated by growth factors and cytokines produced within bone and systemic factors such as parathyroid hormone (PTH) and estrogens (Wein and Kronenberg, 2018; DiGirolamo et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: An imbalance in proportions of bone cells can result in diseases of bone mass such as osteopenia, osteoporosis, and osteopetrosis.
claims.source: An imbalance in proportions of these cells in bone impairs bone resorption and formation, which can result in diseases of bone mass such as osteopenia, osteoporosis, and osteopetrosis (Ayturk et al., 2020; Kenkre and Bassett, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Long bones form by endochondral ossification.
claims.source: Long bones form by endochondral ossification, a process in which chondrocytes differentiate, proliferate, mature, and become hypertrophic, forming a cartilaginous growth plate that coordinates longitudinal bone growth and is recapitulated in fracture repair (Hu et al., 2017; Javaheri et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Hypertrophic cartilage is remodeled by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs).
claims.source: Hypertrophic cartilage is remodeled by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) (reviewed in Tsang and Cheah, 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: The chondrocyte differentiation cascade is coordinated by many transcription factors and signaling pathways, including reciprocal signaling via the parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHRP)-Indian hedgehog (IHH) feedback loop.
claims.source: The chondrocyte differentiation cascade is coordinated by many transcription factors and signaling pathways, including reciprocal signaling via the parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHRP)-Indian hedgehog (IHH) feedback loop (Kronenberg, 2003; Long and Ornitz, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Resting chondrocytes secrete PTHRP, which binds to parathyroid hormone 1 receptor (PTH1R) expressed by pre-hypertrophic chondrocytes, acting to delay their differentiation to hypertrophic chondrocytes (HCs).
claims.source: Resting chondrocytes secrete PTHRP, which binds to parathyroid hormone 1 receptor (PTH1R) expressed by pre-hypertrophic chondrocytes, acting to delay their differentiation to hypertrophic chondrocytes (HCs) (Mizuhashi et al., 2018; Newton et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: HCs specifically produce collagen type X (Col10a1).
claims.source: HCs specifically produce collagen type X (Col10a1), downregulate PTH1R, and undergo distinct phases of cell enlargement for bone elongation (Cooper et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2014a).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: HCs downregulate PTH1R.
claims.source: HCs specifically produce collagen type X (Col10a1), downregulate PTH1R, and undergo distinct phases of cell enlargement for bone elongation (Cooper et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2014a).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Osteoblasts in trabecular bone are derived from HCs in the growth plate and from osteoprogenitors in the perichondrium that accompany invading blood vessels.
claims.source: Recent work has shown that osteoblasts in trabecular bone are derived from HCs in the growth plate and from osteoprogenitors in the perichondrium that accompany invading blood vessels (Yang et al., 2014a; Maes et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: HCs have been shown to contribute to the full spectrum of cells in the osteoblast lineage in endochondral bone, trabeculae, endosteal/endocortical bone, including osteocytes, and, to a minor degree, bone marrow stromal cells and adipocytes.
claims.source: HCs have been shown to contribute to the full spectrum of cells in the osteoblast lineage in endochondral bone, trabeculae, endosteal/endocortical bone, including osteocytes, and, to a minor degree, bone marrow stromal cells and adipocytes (Yang et al., 2014a; Yang et al., 2014b; Park et al., 2015; Tan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: HC transformation to osteoblasts occurs in bone healing.
claims.source: HC transformation to osteoblasts also occurs in bone healing (Hu et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2014a; Yang et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Mice have reduced bone mass as a consequence of ablating β-catenin and Irx3/5 genes specifically in HCs.
claims.source: The functional importance of the HC lineage has been demonstrated in mice, which have reduced bone mass as a consequence of ablating β-catenin and Irx3/5 genes specifically in HCs (Tan et al., 2020; Houben et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Clustering analyses of the P6 tibia scRNAseq data identified 12 populations, which included eight chondro-osteogenic clusters and four other cell types.
claims.source: Clustering analyses of the P6 tibia scRNAseq data, identified 12 populations, which, from their molecular signatures, included eight chondro-osteogenic clusters and four other cell types (Figure 1B and 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Five chondrogenic clusters were annotated as resting, proliferating, maturing, pre-hypertrophic, and hypertrophic chondrocytes based on molecular signatures.
claims.source: By calculating the cluster signatures and referencing known markers in the literature (Tan et al., 2018; Tikhonova et al., 2019; Wai et al., 1998), we annotated the five chondrogenic clusters as resting (e.g., Pthlh), proliferating (e.g., Top2a, Mki67), maturing (e.g., Col9a2, Matn1), pre-hypertrophic (pre-HCs) (e.g., Ihh, Fgfr3, Pth1r), and hypertrophic chondrocytes (Col10a1) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data and comparison with known markers from the literature.

claims.claim: Three osteogenic clusters were identified as immature and mature osteoblasts, and osteocytes.
claims.source: Similarly, the three osteogenic clusters were identified as immature (Mmp14, Pdgfrb) and mature (Ifitm5, Bglap) osteoblasts, and osteocytes (corresponding to terminally differentiated osteoblasts, Sost1, Dmp1, Phex) (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, and 'Materials and methods').
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: 18.1% of immature osteoblasts were estimated to be HC-derived (tdTomato expressing).
claims.source: Immature osteoblasts represent an important early stage in the HC to osteoblast transition and 18.1% of them were estimated to be HC-derived (tdTomato expressing) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of tdTomato expression in single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claims.claim: Mmp13 was expressed in both the HC and immature Ob populations.
claims.source: Amongst the Mmp's, Mmp13 was expressed in both the HC and immature Ob populations (Figure 1C, Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 1—source data 3; Yang et al., 2014a; Tan et al., 2018), consistent with the literature (Stickens et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA sequencing data and is consistent with prior literature.

claims.claim: Mmp14 was not expressed in HCs but was enriched in immature osteoblasts.
claims.source: By contrast,Mmp14, which encodes a membrane-anchored MMP (Zhou et al., 2000), was not expressed in HCs but was enriched in immature osteoblasts (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Immunostaining for MMP14 detected no protein in HCs and strong expression in LacZ-labeled HC-descendant cells, especially those located at the chondro-osseous junction.
claims.source: Consistent with the scRNAseq results, immunostaining for MMP14 detected no protein in HCs and strong expression in LacZ-labeled HC-descendant cells, especially those located at the chondro-osseous junction (Figure 1D) (identified by co-staining with LacZ in C10Cre; Rosa26LSL-LacZ/LSL-LacZ [RLacZ] mice; Yang et al., 2014a).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Four osteoblast subpopulations were identified at P56, including osteo-progenitors, immature osteoblasts, proliferating osteoblasts, and mature osteoblasts.
claims.source: We focused on the 1256 osteogenic cells of P6 and P56 combined, wherein four subpopulations were identified, including osteo-progenitors (marked by Grem1, Vcam1, Lpl, Steap4, and Col4a1/2), immature osteoblasts (Postn, Slc20a2), proliferating osteoblasts (Top2a, Mki67, and Birc5), and mature osteoblasts (Bglap, Phex, Dmp1, Col22a1, Ifitm5, and Smpd3) (Figure 1H and L, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I, Figure 1—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on integrated analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data from P6 and P56 samples.

claims.claim: The P56 sample had much fewer proliferating osteoblasts (only 1 cell, or 0.2%) than the P6 sample (190 cells, or 6%).
claims.source: Interestingly, although both P6 (6.8%, or 215 out of 3163 cells) and P56 (9.8%, or 42 out of 408 cells) retained certain proportions of proliferating chondrocytes (Figure 1G), the P56 had much fewer proliferating osteoblasts (only 1 cell, or 0.2%) than the P6 (190 cells, or 6%) (Figure 1I, Figure 1—source data 3), which probably reflects maturation of the osteoblast lineage by P56.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of cell populations in single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claims.claim: 23.8% of the P6 and 31.6% of the P56 osteogenic cells were HC-derived.
claims.source: Overall, 23.8% of the P6 and 31.6% of the P56 osteogenic cells were HC-derived.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of tdTomato-expressing cells in single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claims.claim: 38 genes were differentially expressed between HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblasts, with 10 genes expressed higher in the HC-derived and 28 genes in the non-HC-derived.
claims.source: We also assessed how similar HC-derived and non-HC-derived cells are, and detected the 38 genes (Figure 1—source data 4) that were differentially expressed between the two lineages, with 10 genes expressed higher in the HC-derived and 28 genes in the non-HC-derived (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
claims.evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claims.claim: There was a broad similarity in transcriptomic characteristics for the HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblasts.
claims.source: Overall, there was a broad similarity in transcriptomic characteristics for the HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblasts.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of single-cell RNA sequencing data showing only 38 differentially expressed genes.

claims.claim: Global Mmp13 knockout mice display abnormal growth plates with disrupted terminal hypertrophy and increased trabecular bone.
claims.source: Global Mmp13 knockout mice display abnormal growth plates with disrupted terminal hypertrophy and increased trabecular bone which could reflect an impact on the HC-Ob lineage continuum.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature.

claims.claim: Col1a1-cre conditional Mmp13 knockout mice showed increased trabecular bone.
claims.source: However, while Col1a1-cre conditional (acting on osteoblasts) Mmp13 knockout mice showed increased trabecular bone, Col2a1-cre Mmp13 conditional mutants (acting on chondrocytes and perichondrium) did not, but displayed trabecular bone irregularities that were attributed to remodeling defects (Stickens et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature (Stickens et al., 2004).

claims.claim: Mmp14 null mutants display the most severe skeletal phenotypes amongst MMPs, including loss of trabecular bone, over-activity of osteoclasts, impaired angiogenesis, and reduced calvarial ossification.
claims.source: Amongst MMPs, Mmp14 null mutants display the most severe skeletal phenotypes, including loss of trabecular bone, over-activity of osteoclasts, impaired angiogenesis, and reduced calvarial ossification (Zhou et al., 2000; Holmbeck et al., 1999; Hikita et al., 2006; Chan et al., 2012), consistent with expression of Mmp14 by many cell types, such as skeletal progenitors, osteoblasts, osteoclasts, endothelial cells, and bone marrow stromal cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Chan et al., 2012; Jin et al., 2011; Gonzalo et al., 2010; Langlois et al., 2004; Attur et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: >75% of both HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblast lineages co-expressed Mmp14+/Pth1r+.
claims.source: Interestingly, Mmp14 is co-expressed with Pth1r, a key regulator of chondrocyte hypertrophy and osteogenesis (Calvi et al., 2001; Hirai et al., 2011; Lanske et al., 1999), where >75% of both HC-derived and non-HC-derived lineages co-expressed Mmp14+/Pth1r+ (Figure 1L and M).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of co-expression in single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1M.

claims.claim: There was an increased accumulation of HC descendants at the chondro-osseous junction in global Mmp14 knockout mice compared to WT controls.
claims.source: We used the C10Cre; Rosa26LSL-YFP/LSL-YFP(RYFP) reporter to lineage trace HC derivatives in global Mmp14 knockout mice and found an increased accumulation of HC descendants at the chondro-osseous junction compared to WT controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This is based on lineage tracing and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: There was a small increase in proliferating HC-derivatives (marked by EdU) in the region immediately below the chondro-osseous junction in Mmp14 knockout mice.
claims.source: There was also a small increase in proliferating HC-derivatives (marked by 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine [Edu]) in the region immediately below the chondro-osseous junction (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is based on EdU labeling and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: There were fewer proliferating HC-derivatives in distal regions below the chondro-osseous junction in Mmp14 knockout mice, consistent with their accumulation and impaired translocation into the trabecular bone.
claims.source: However, there were fewer proliferating HC-derivatives in further distal regions below the chondro-osseous junction, consistent with their accumulation there and impaired translocation into the trabecular bone (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is based on EdU labeling and quantification, with inference about impaired translocation.

claims.claim: Removing Mmp14 in HC-descendants did not recapitulate the accumulation of HC descendants at the chondro-osseous junction observed in Mmp14-/- mice.
claims.source: We found that removing Mmp14 in HC-descendants did not recapitulate the accumulation of HC descendants at the chondro-osseous junction observed in Mmp14-/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of lineage-specific and global knockout phenotypes.

claims.claim: The localization and distribution of HC-descendants were unaffected in Mmp14ΔHC mice.
claims.source: We used tamoxifen-mediated pulse-labeling and chasing of Mmp14-deficient HC descendants using C10Cre-ERT;Mmp14F/F; Rtdt to assay the dynamics of their translocation into the subchondral space. We found that the localization and distribution of HC-descendants were unaffected in Mmp14ΔHC mice (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is based on lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The aberrant stagnation of HC derivatives at the chondro-osseous junction was not intrinsic to a defect in these cells themselves but might be a consequence of MMP14 deficiency elsewhere.
claims.source: These results suggest the aberrant stagnation of HC derivatives at the chondro-osseous junction was not intrinsic to a defect in these cells themselves but might be a consequence of MMP14 deficiency elsewhere, for example, in the invading vascular cells and/or the accompanying osteoprogenitors from the perichondrium that co-migrate with blood vessels to populate the primary spongiosa (Maes et al., 2010; Kusumbe et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of global and conditional knockout phenotypes.

claims.claim: Both vascular density and endothelial cell count (measured using the marker ENDOMUCIN) were decreased in Mmp14-/- mice compared with control mice.
claims.source: We therefore examined the vascular capillaries in Mmp14-/- mice and found that both vascular density and endothelial cell count (measured using the marker ENDOMUCIN) were decreased compared with control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: Mmp14 is important for angiogenesis, neovessel formation and migration in vitro and in vivo.
claims.source: In vitro and in vivo studies have shown that Mmp14 is important for angiogenesis, neovessel formation and migration (Zhou et al., 2000; Chun et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature.

claims.claim: The abnormal vascularization in Mmp14 null mice may be a major contributor to the compromised translocation of HC-derived cells to the trabecular bone.
claims.source: The abnormal vascularization in Mmp14 null mice may therefore be a major contributor to the compromised translocation of HC-derived cells to the trabecular bone.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed vascularization defects and translocation phenotype.

claims.claim: MicroCT analysis revealed a 16% increase in BMD and a 10% increase in trabecular BV/TV in Mmp14ΔHC mice at P10.
claims.source: Interestingly, microCT analysis revealed a 16% increase in BMD and a 10% increase in trabecular BV/TV in Mmp14ΔHC mice (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is based on microCT analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The number of HC descendants was increased in Mmp14ΔHC mice at P10.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence staining of MMP14 and RFP shows the number of HC descendants was increased in Mmp14ΔHC mice at P10 (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining and quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The increase in HC descendants in Mmp14ΔHC mice could be due to a decrease of TUNEL+ cells at the chondro-osseous junction.
claims.source: This observation could be due to a decrease of TUNEL+ cells at the chondro-osseous junction (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is based on TUNEL assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: An increased number of HC-derived osteoblasts was observed in Mmp14ΔHC mutants, compared to similar GFP+ RFP- cell counts between mutants and controls.
claims.source: By using C1-GFP transgene to co-label osteoblasts, we observed an increased number of HC-derived osteoblasts in Mmp14ΔHC mutants, compared to similar GFP+ RFP cell counts between mutants and controls (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining and quantification shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Targeting Mmp14 in HCs promoted osteogenesis.
claims.source: The data collectively suggests targeting Mmp14 in HCs promoted osteogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the increased number of HC-derived osteoblasts and bone mass in Mmp14ΔHC mutants.

claims.claim: The number of Edu+-labeled proliferating cells was comparable between Mmp14ΔHC mutants and control mice.
claims.source: In contrast to reduced apoptotic cells, the number of Edu+-labeled proliferating cells was comparable between Mmp14ΔHC mutants and control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on EdU labeling and quantification shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The number of osteoclasts was comparable between Mmp14ΔHC mutants and controls at P10.
claims.source: In line with reports showing MMP14 deficiency does not affect osteoclastogenesis (Tang et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2020), the number of osteoclasts was comparable between Mmp14ΔHC mutants and controls at P10, suggesting the increased number of HC-derived osteogenic cells, not reduced resorption, was a major contributor for increased bone mass at this stage.
claims.evidence: This is based on TRAP staining and quantification, consistent with prior literature.

claims.claim: The total frequency of HC-derived bone marrow adipocytes in Mmp14ΔHC mice was unchanged compared with control.
claims.source: We found that the total frequency of HC-derived bone marrow adipocytes in Mmp14ΔHC mice was unchanged compared with control, suggesting that MMP14 does not influence the adipogenic fate choice of HC-derived cells.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of adipocytes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: MMP14 was shown to be a downstream target of PTH signaling in osteocytes.
claims.source: Interestingly, MMP14 was shown to be a downstream target of PTH signaling in osteocytes (Delgado-Calle et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature.

claims.claim: Cleavage of PTH1R can be inhibited by TIMP2, but not TIMP1.
claims.source: It has been proposed that, because cleavage of PTH1R can be inhibited by TIMP2, but not TIMP1, MMP-dependent cleavage of PTH1R causes reduced stability and degradation of PTH1R, raising the possibility that cleavage by an MMP might inhibit PTH signaling (Klenk et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature (Klenk et al., 2010).

claims.claim: In the presence of MT1-FL, a truncated form of PTH1R-HA with size close to 55 kDa is increased compared to empty vector and MT1-EA.
claims.source: After deglycosylation with PNGaseF, western blotting showed, in the presence of MT1-FL, a truncated form of PTH1R-HA with size close to 55 kDa is increased compared to empty vector and MT1-EA (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on western blotting data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: A truncated protein fragment of PTH1R was detected when MT1-FL was expressed with mouse Pth1r without HA-tag.
claims.source: To exclude that the cleavage is an artifact due to HA-tag insertion in the extracellular domain, a mouse Pth1r cDNA without HA-tag was reverse transcribed from extracted RNA and cloned into pcDNA3.1 expression vector (Figure 3C). Like PTH1R-HA, a truncated protein fragment of PTH1R was detected when MT1-FL was expressed, confirming proteolytic processing of PTH1R exists both in mice and human (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on western blotting data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: rhMMP14 directly cleaves PTH1R-ECD at multiple sites.
claims.source: Western blots showed, compared to full-length deglycosylated PTH1R-ECD, after incubation with rhMMP14 (lane 2), there appeared at 25 kDa (lane 3), two truncated fragments with size around 20 kDa and 15 kDa (Figure 3D). These results suggest that rhMMP14 directly cleaves PTH1R-ECD at multiple sites, with one cleavage site at around amino acid 60 and another at around 90–100, accounting for the two histidine-tagged fragments detected by SDS-PAGE observed (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is based on in vitro cleavage assay and western blotting shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Blocking MMP14 activity by EDTA inhibited PTH1R cleavage.
claims.source: Blocking MMP14 activity by EDTA inhibited PTH1R cleavage (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is based on in vitro cleavage assay with EDTA shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: ADAM10, ADAM15, and ADAM17 did not cleave PTH1R.
claims.source: To test if other MMPs/ADAMs participate in the cleavage of PTH1R, we assayed ADAM10, ADAM15, and ADAM17 and found none of them cleaved (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on western blotting assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: MMP14 can interact with PTH1R.
claims.source: Co-immunoprecipitation of PTH1R-HA and MT1-FL suggested that MMP14 can interact with PTH1R (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C.

claims.claim: A truncated 55 kDa form of PTH1R can be detected in the Mmp14+/+ trabecular bone lysates but not in those from Mmp14-/- mutants.
claims.source: To test if MMP14 cleavage of PTH1R occurred in vivo, trabecular bone protein lysate was prepared from wild-type and Mmp14-/- mice at P14. A truncated 55 kDa form of PTH1R can be detected in the Mmp14+/+ trabecular bone lysates but not in those from Mmp14-/- mutants suggesting MMP14 may be the sole protease/MMP that cleaves PTH1R in osteogenic cells (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is based on western blotting of trabecular bone lysates shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: MMP14 may be the sole protease/MMP that cleaves PTH1R in osteogenic cells.
claims.source: A truncated 55 kDa form of PTH1R can be detected in the Mmp14+/+ trabecular bone lysates but not in those from Mmp14-/- mutants suggesting MMP14 may be the sole protease/MMP that cleaves PTH1R in osteogenic cells (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of cleaved PTH1R in Mmp14-/- lysates.

claims.claim: Mass spectrometry found a peak at 770 Da consistent with molecular mass of a VLQRPAS fragment, suggesting that amino acid 61 is one of the cleavage sites of MMP14.
claims.source: To test this, we incubated rhMMP14 with a synthetic peptide with amino acid sequence 55–67 from PTH1R. Using mass spectrometry, we found a peak at 770 Da consistent with molecular mass of a VLQRPAS fragment, suggesting that amino acid 61 is one of the cleavage sites of MMP14 (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Lower relative amounts of p-CREB, p-ERK, and cyclic-AMP (cAMP) were observed after PTH challenge in 293T cells expressing MT1-FL compared to control.
claims.source: As expected, lower relative amounts of p-CREB, p-ERK, and cyclic-AMP (cAMP) were observed after PTH challenge in 293T cells expressing MT1-FL compared to control, suggesting that MMP14 inhibits PTH signaling by facilitating receptor degradation (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is based on western blotting and cAMP assays shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: MMP14 inhibits PTH signaling by facilitating receptor degradation.
claims.source: As expected, lower relative amounts of p-CREB, p-ERK, and cyclic-AMP (cAMP) were observed after PTH challenge in 293T cells expressing MT1-FL compared to control, suggesting that MMP14 inhibits PTH signaling by facilitating receptor degradation (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in PTH signaling markers when MMP14 is present.

claims.claim: MMP14 deficient primary trabecular osteoblasts showed increased p-CREB activity in response to PTH.
claims.source: We isolated trabecular osteoblasts from Mmp14-/- mice in order to ensure only MMP14-deficient cells were analyzed. These MMP14 deficient primary trabecular osteoblasts showed increased p-CREB activity in response to PTH (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is based on western blotting of primary osteoblasts shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Increasing MT1-FL further promoted PTH1R degradation.
claims.source: We titrated the level of MT1-FL against the same amount of PTH1R and found increasing MT1-FL further promoted PTH1R degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is based on western blotting with titration of MMP14 shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: MMP14 is upregulated in response to PTH treatment.
claims.source: Consistent with previous reports, MMP14 is upregulated in response to PTH treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and is consistent with prior reports.

claims.claim: Cleavage of PTH1R by MMP14 at amino acid 61 is a novel mechanism for modulating GPCR stability and attenuating PTH signaling.
claims.source: Overall, these results identify cleavage of PTH1R by MMP14 at amino acid 61 as a novel mechanism for modulating GPCR stability and subsequently attenuated PTH signaling (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective data showing MMP14 cleavage of PTH1R and its effects on signaling.

claims.claim: Compared to PTH stimulation in WT controls, PTH treatment in Mmp14ΔHC mutants caused a 15 and 21% further increase in BMD and BV/TV, respectively.
claims.source: Compared to PTH stimulation in WT controls, PTH treatment in Mmp14ΔHC mutants caused a 15 and 21% further increase in BMD and BV/TV, respectively (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: This is based on microCT analysis of PTH-treated mice shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: PTH treatment dramatically increased the amount of HC progeny (tdT+) in Mmp14ΔHC trabecular bone.
claims.source: PTH treatment dramatically increased the amount of HC progeny (tdT+, detected by RFP immunostaining) in Mmp14ΔHC trabecular bone (Figure 5B and C).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining and quantification shown in Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: Many more HC descendants in the trabecular region co-expressed OSTERIX and C1-GFP in response to PTH treatment than in controls.
claims.source: We found many more HC descendants in the trabecular region that co-expressed OSTERIX, a marker of osteoprogenitors, and C1-GFP in response to PTH treatment than in controls (Figure 6A and B).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining and quantification shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: HC descendants showed positive pCREB+RFP+ staining confirming PTH signaling activity in HC derivatives.
claims.source: These HC descendants showed positive pCREB+RFP+ staining confirming PTH signaling activity in HC derivatives (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: HC-derived cells constituted approximately 50% of all trabecular osteoblasts with and without PTH treatment.
claims.source: HC-derived cells constituted approximately 50% of all trabecular osteoblasts with and without PTH treatment (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of HC-derived osteoblasts shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: HC-derived osteoblasts represent a significant osteogenic population directly contributing to half of the total osteoblast population and capable of responding to PTH treatment in the same way as non-HC-derived osteoblasts.
claims.source: HC-derived osteoblasts therefore represent a significant osteogenic population directly contributing to half of the total osteoblast population and capable of responding to PTH treatment in the same way as non-HC-derived osteoblasts (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the quantification showing ~50% contribution and similar response to PTH.

claims.claim: In Mmp14ΔHC mice, the number of RFP+ and RFP+ GFP+ and RFP+ OSX+ cells further increased compared to control mice treated with PTH.
claims.source: In Mmp14ΔHC mice, the number of RFP+ and RFP+ GFP+ and RFP+ OSX+ cells further increased compared to control mice treated with PTH, consistent with the heightened response to PTH treatment in Mmp14-deficient HC-derived cells (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: BV/TV and cortical BMD were comparable between PTH-treated Mmp14ΔHC mutants compared to PTH-treated controls.
claims.source: By contrast with enhanced osteogenesis in trabecular bone, BV/TV and cortical BMD were comparable between PTH-treated Mmp14ΔHC mutants compared to PTH-treated controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

results.result: Single-cell transcriptomics reveals that HC-derived cells activate MMP14 as they transition to osteoblasts, with MMP14 enriched in immature osteoblasts but not in hypertrophic chondrocytes. HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblasts show broad transcriptomic similarity with only 38 differentially expressed genes, and >75% of both populations co-express Mmp14 and Pth1r.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C26-C37, C41, and C104 collectively demonstrate through single-cell RNA sequencing at P6 and P56 that MMP14 is specifically activated in HC-derived immature osteoblasts at the chondro-osseous junction (C31, C32), with immunostaining validation (C32). The transcriptomic similarity between HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblasts (only 38 DEGs, C36-C37) and high co-expression of Mmp14/Pth1r (C41) are well-supported by the scRNAseq data presented in Figure 1.

results.result: HC lineage-specific deletion of Mmp14 (Mmp14ΔHC) results in increased bone mass at P10, with a 16% increase in BMD and 10% increase in BV/TV, due to increased HC-derived osteoblasts and reduced apoptosis rather than changes in proliferation, osteoclast numbers, or adipogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C45-C46, C51-C58, and C105 are well-supported by microCT data (C51), immunofluorescence quantification (C52, C54), TUNEL assays (C53), and TRAP staining (C57). The phenotype contrasts with global Mmp14 knockout (C3, C45), demonstrating cell-autonomous effects. Controls for proliferation (C56), osteoclasts (C57), and adipogenesis (C58) strengthen the conclusion that increased osteogenesis is the primary mechanism.

results.result: Global Mmp14 knockout mice show accumulation of HC descendants at the chondro-osseous junction with impaired translocation to trabecular bone, likely due to defective vascularization rather than intrinsic HC defects, as vascular density and endothelial cell counts are decreased in Mmp14-/- mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44, C47-C50 are supported by lineage tracing (C42), EdU labeling (C43-C44), and vascular analysis (C48). The inference that vascularization defects contribute to HC accumulation (C47, C50) is reasonable given the established role of MMP14 in angiogenesis (C49) and the contrast with Mmp14ΔHC mice where HC translocation is normal (C45-C46).

results.result: MMP14 directly cleaves PTH1R at amino acid 61 in the extracellular domain, as demonstrated by in vitro cleavage assays with recombinant proteins, cell-based assays, mass spectrometry, and detection of cleaved PTH1R in wild-type but not Mmp14-/- trabecular bone lysates.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C61-C69 are strongly supported by multiple complementary approaches: western blotting with full-length and catalytically inactive MMP14 (C61-C62), in vitro cleavage with recombinant proteins (C63-C64), specificity testing with other proteases (C65), co-immunoprecipitation (C66), in vivo validation (C67-C68), and mass spectrometry identification of the cleavage site (C69). The convergence of evidence from cell-free, cell-based, and in vivo systems provides robust support.

results.result: MMP14 cleavage of PTH1R dampens PTH signaling by promoting receptor degradation, as evidenced by reduced p-CREB, p-ERK, and cAMP levels in cells expressing MMP14, and increased p-CREB activity in Mmp14-/- primary osteoblasts following PTH challenge.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C70-C75 are well-supported by cell-based assays showing reduced PTH signaling markers (p-CREB, p-ERK, cAMP) when MMP14 is present (C70) and increased signaling in Mmp14-/- cells (C72). The dose-dependent effect (C73) and upregulation of MMP14 by PTH (C74) support the proposed regulatory mechanism. The inference that cleavage promotes degradation (C71) is reasonable given the observed reduction in receptor levels and signaling.

results.result: HC-derived osteoblasts contribute approximately 50% of PTH-stimulated osteogenesis in trabecular bone, responding to PTH treatment similarly to non-HC-derived osteoblasts, with this response amplified in Mmp14ΔHC mutants showing 15% and 21% further increases in BMD and BV/TV respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C76-C82, C101, C121-C122 are supported by quantitative immunofluorescence showing ~50% HC-derived contribution (C80), increased osteoblast markers (C78), p-CREB staining confirming PTH signaling (C79), and microCT data showing enhanced response in Mmp14ΔHC mutants (C76-C77). The convergence of lineage tracing, signaling markers, and bone mass measurements provides strong support for the ~50% contribution and amplified response in mutants.

results.result: HC-derived osteoblasts maintain their ability to respond to PTH treatment with aging, as demonstrated by increased osteogenic progeny production in response to PTH(1-34) in both young (P10) and 1-year-old mice, with continued MMP14 expression in these cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C89-C91, C123 are supported by quantification of HC-derived osteoblasts in PTH-treated mice at different ages (C89, C123) and immunofluorescence showing MMP14 expression in aged mice (C91). The data demonstrate sustained responsiveness across ages, though the limited age range (P10 to 1 year) and lack of data from very old mice (2+ years) noted in the discussion represents a limitation.

results.result: The MMP14-mediated control of PTH signaling likely applies to both HC-derived and non-HC-derived osteoblasts due to their transcriptomic similarity and co-expression of Mmp14 and Pth1r.
results.evaluation: Claims C9 and C126 are supported by the transcriptomic data showing broad similarity (only 38 DEGs, C36-C37) and >75% co-expression of Mmp14/Pth1r in both populations (C41). However, the inference is limited by the lack of direct functional testing in non-HC-derived osteoblasts, as acknowledged by the authors. The claim is reasonable but represents an extrapolation from the HC-specific experiments.

results.result: In cortical bone, PTH treatment effects differ from trabecular bone, with comparable BV/TV and BMD between Mmp14ΔHC mutants and controls, though HC-derived osteocytes show enhanced PTH response in mutants and increased CyclinD and Runx2 expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C88 are supported by microCT analysis (C83) and immunofluorescence quantification (C84-C88). The data show tissue-specific differences in PTH response, with cortical bone showing less dramatic effects than trabecular bone. The increased expression of CyclinD and Runx2 (C86) and enhanced osteocyte response (C88) suggest some MMP14 effects in cortical bone, but the overall bone mass effects are muted compared to trabecular bone.

results.result: The study establishes a novel paradigm where MMP14 modulates PTH signaling intensity in the HC-osteoblast lineage through direct cleavage of PTH1R, thereby controlling the supply of osteoblast precursors and bone anabolism, with genetic targeting of MMP14 boosting PTH-mediated bone synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C103, C106, C115-C117, C127 represent the integrated conclusions of the study, synthesizing the molecular mechanism (MMP14 cleavage of PTH1R), cellular effects (enhanced PTH signaling in Mmp14ΔHC), and physiological outcomes (increased bone formation). These conclusions are well-supported by the convergence of biochemical, cellular, and in vivo evidence presented throughout the manuscript.

results.result: MMP14 may be involved in a negative feedback mechanism to constrain osteogenesis in response to PTH challenge, based on its upregulation by PTH signaling.
results.evaluation: Claim C119 is speculative, as acknowledged by the authors ('it is possible'). While the upregulation of MMP14 by PTH (C74, C118) is demonstrated, the negative feedback mechanism is inferred rather than directly tested. Additional experiments manipulating MMP14 levels during PTH treatment would be needed to confirm this regulatory loop.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the biological context through established knowledge about bone homeostasis, endochondral ossification, HC-derived osteoblasts, PTH signaling, MMP14 functions, and prior work on related pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C10-C25, C38-C40, C49, C59-C60, C92, C94-C100, C107-C108, C110, C112-C113, C118, C124-C125 represent background knowledge and prior work that is appropriately cited and accurately represented. These claims provide the scientific foundation for the current study and are supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Supporting observations include Mmp13 expression in both HCs and immature osteoblasts, normal osteoclastogenesis in Mmp14ΔHC mutants, no effect on HC-derived adipocyte frequency, proteolytic modification of PTH1R affecting GPCR stability, and potential relevance to human Olliers disease mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C93, C109, C111, C114, C120 represent supporting observations and interpretations. C30 is supported by scRNAseq data; C109 and C111 by quantification showing no changes in osteoclasts or adipocytes; C114 by the collective biochemical data; and C120 by literature on human mutations. C93 is a hypothesis that guided the experimental design and is supported by the subsequent findings.
